US.liability: Report within 2 business days of learning of the loss: max $50. After 2 business days: up to $500. Unauthorized transfer on a statement: report within 60 days of the statement or you may be liable for later transfers. Extended for extenuating circumstances (travel, hospitalization).

UK.notification_deadline: Regulation 74: must notify the payment service provider without undue delay on becoming aware of the unauthorised transaction, and no later than 13 months after the debit date.
UK.refund_timing: Regulation 76: the provider must refund the unauthorised amount and restore the account "as soon as practicable, and in any event no later than the end of the business day following the day on which it becomes aware of the unauthorised transaction", unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and notifies the relevant authority in writing.
UK.liability_cap: Regulation 77: the payer's liability is capped at £35, except where the loss/theft was undetectable before payment (unless the payer acted fraudulently), was caused by the provider's employee/agent, or the payer acted fraudulently or with intent/gross negligence (cap does not apply in those cases).
UK.complaint_route: Complain to the firm first — it has 15 days to respond to complaints about payment services, fraud/scams or e-money (8 weeks for most other complaints). You then have 6 months from the date of the firm's final response to refer the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

EU.notification_deadline: Article 71(1): must notify the payment service provider without undue delay on becoming aware of the unauthorised or incorrectly executed transaction, and no later than 13 months after the debit date.
EU.refund_timing: Article 73(1): the payer's payment service provider must refund the amount "immediately, and in any event no later than by the end of the following business day, after noting or being notified of the transaction", except where it has reasonable grounds for suspecting fraud and communicates those grounds to the relevant national authority in writing.
EU.liability_cap: Article 74(1): the payer may be obliged to bear losses up to a maximum of EUR 50 resulting from use of a lost/stolen payment instrument or misappropriation; does not apply where the loss was undetectable before payment (unless the payer acted fraudulently) or was caused by an employee/agent/branch of the provider. Article 74(2): where the provider does not require strong customer authentication, the payer bears no financial loss unless they acted fraudulently.

US.rule: CFPB "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions" rule — NOT currently in force
US.status_note: On May 12, 2025, the President signed a joint resolution passed by Congress disapproving the Final Rule entitled "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions." Consistent with the joint resolution, the Final Rule has no force or effect. The remainder of Regulations E and Z are unchanged and remain in force and effect.
US.current_status: As of the verification date there is no CFPB overdraft-fee cap or junk-fee rule for very large financial institutions in force; standard Regulation E and Regulation Z protections remain in force.

UK.rule: FCA Handbook CONC 5C (Overdraft pricing), in force since 6 April 2020
UK.requirements: CONC 5C.2.1R(3): "The rate of interest that applies to any given balance of arranged overdraft relating to a personal current account must either be zero or the same as the rate of interest that applies to any other balance of arranged overdraft in respect of that personal current account" (a single simple annual interest rate, no fixed daily/monthly fees). CONC 5C.2.2G(1): firms are forbidden from imposing a fee for making available an arranged overdraft facility (unless the credit made available exceeds £10,000). CONC 5C.2.1R(6): unarranged overdraft charges must be structured and presented in the same way as arranged ones (the rate may be lower, but not charged as a separate higher fee structure).

EU.requirements: Banks must give consumers a "fee information document" listing fees for the most commonly used services before they sign a contract to open an account, and a "statement of fees" of all charges incurred, free of charge, at least annually. Member States must ensure consumers have free access to at least one independent, up-to-date bank fee comparison website. Under Article 10, when switching accounts within the same Member State, the receiving provider must request the transfer from the old provider within 2 business days of getting the consumer's authorisation, and standing orders/direct debits on the new account must start no earlier than 6 business days after the receiving provider gets the transferred documents.

US.steps: Dispute in writing with the credit bureau (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) AND the furnisher (e.g. your bank). Furnishers generally must investigate and respond within 30 days. Bureau must forward your dispute to the furnisher and report results back. If it rules the dispute frivolous it must send notice within 5 business days. If the furnisher says it's accurate, you can add a statement to your file. Escalate: CFPB complaint; identity theft: IdentityTheft.gov.

UK.rule: ICO guidance on correcting your credit file (Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR)
UK.response_deadline: "By law the agency must tell you within 28 days of your letter if it has: removed the entry from your file; amended the entry; or taken no action."
UK.notice_of_correction: If the agency doesn't reply within 28 days, or replies but takes no action, you can ask it to add a "notice of correction" — a statement of up to 200 words explaining why you think the entry is wrong, which will be seen by anyone who looks at that entry.
UK.escalation: You can contact the Information Commissioner if the issue isn't resolved. If the agency considers a notice of correction incorrect, defamatory, frivolous or otherwise unsuitable for publication, it must pass it to the Information Commissioner, who will order what notice, if any, should be added.

US.summary: Collectors may not harass, oppress or abuse you; repetitious, excessive or threatening communications are covered. At first contact or within 5 days they generally must give creditor name, amount owed and how to dispute. In certain situations you have 30 days to request information. You can tell a collector in writing to stop contacting you (CFPB provides a sample letter). Keep copies. Complain at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or 855-411-2372.

UK.rule: FCA Handbook CONC 7 (Arrears, default and recovery, including repossessions)
UK.requirements: CONC 7.3.4R: firms must treat customers in or approaching arrears or default with forbearance and due consideration. CONC 7.3.10R: a firm must not pressurise a customer to pay in one or very few repayments, to pay within an unreasonably short time, or to raise funds by selling property/borrowing. CONC 7.3.14R: a firm must not take disproportionate action against a customer in arrears or default. CONC 7.3.17R: a firm must not repossess a customer's home, goods or vehicles other than as a last resort. CONC 7.3.11R / 7.3.12G: a firm must suspend active pursuit of debt recovery for a "reasonable period" (generally 30 days, extendable by a further 30) while the customer is developing a repayment plan.
UK.complaint_route: "Before bringing your complaint to us, you should make a formal complaint to the company involved. If they don't send you a final response letter within eight weeks – or you're unhappy with their response – you can bring the complaint to us."

US.rule: Fair Credit Billing Act (FCBA), implemented via Regulation Z
US.dispute_window: "Send your written notice no later than 60 days after the credit card company sent the statement where the error first appeared."
US.issuer_deadlines: "Once you point out a mistake on your bill, the credit card company has 30 days to tell you it got your letter. It gets another two billing cycles to finish looking into your dispute." You don't have to pay the disputed amount, or related finance/other charges, while it's under investigation.
US.unauthorized_charge_cap: "If there is unauthorized use of your card before you report it missing, the most you will owe for unauthorized charges on the card is $50." If you report a lost/stolen card before it's used, or only your account number (not the physical card) was stolen, you generally have no liability.

UK.rule: Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 (credit cards) and chargeback (voluntary card-scheme protection)
UK.section_75: "If you use your credit card to buy something costing more than £100 and up to £30,000, you're covered by 'section 75' of the Consumer Credit Act... This means the credit card company has equal responsibility (or 'liability') with the seller if there's a problem with the things you've bought or the company you've bought them from fails." Applies even if only part of the price (e.g. a deposit) was paid by credit card. Does not apply to debit cards.
UK.chargeback: "Chargeback isn't legal protection like section 75... It's an agreement Visa, Mastercard and American Express have signed up to... You must make a claim within 120 days of making the purchase. If the purchase is for something in the future, for example, tickets to an event, the 120-day limit starts from the day the event would have happened." Works for debit, credit or prepaid cards.
UK.complaint_route: If not satisfied with the card company's response, you can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
